description: Database access, keyed on the port of a local tunnel. When a database sits in a private network and the only working path is a local tunnel on a known port, gating the hostname alone locks the path that cannot work and leaves the one that works open. So the rules look for the tunnel port. Set <DEV_PORT>, <PROD_PORT> and <PROD_HOST> in ~/.claude/guardrails/placeholders.json (see examples/placeholders.json). An unset placeholder matches nothing, so these rules stay inert until you set them. A read-only wrapper (here `db-readonly`, which opens every session with SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY) stays tier 2 on any port: a read cannot mutate data.

rules._comment: Read-only wrapper: tier 2 (audited, no unlock) on any port. MUST stay above the port rules.

PROD tunnel, client form: a database client in command position (after normalisation of sudo, env, absolute paths) with the port in its arguments. No SQL-verb parsing: `-c 'select 1; UPDATE ...'` splits across segments and a verb regex would only see the harmless half. A doc line that opens with `psql ... -p <PROD_PORT>` still trips it. That is the fail-closed side of the trade, and the read path is free.
PROD tunnel, environment form: any assignment that carries the port (DATABASE_URL=postgres://...:<PROD_PORT>/app cargo run, export PGPORT=<PROD_PORT>).
DEV tunnel, same two forms. A shared team database: tier 3, so it is denied headless, but internal, so it passes silently with a human in front.

Anti-bypass: a client aimed straight at the production host, by flag or by URL. Patterns are POSIX ERE: a PCRE lookahead such as (?!localhost) never compiles in bash, and the guard now reports such a pattern as a misconfiguration.
